channel.title: Oleksandr Shepotylo
channel.description: What trade policy actually does at the level of the firm.

item.title: After SPS: the EU trade barrier that needs fixing next
item.description:
Drawing on five years of monthly bilateral trade data across 100 countries (2017–2025), this piece finds that while deeply integrated sectors like pharmaceuticals and automotive components have proven more resilient to Brexit than consumer goods, the underlying commercial logic of running cross-border production under two regulatory regimes is weakening year on year. Overall, UK exports to the EU have seen a 53.8% decline in product varieties and a 16.5% fall in value, with technical barriers — conformity assessment and dual certification in particular — imposing disproportionate costs on the most interconnected sectors. The recommendation is a sectoral mutual recognition agreement modelled on the EU–Switzerland framework, alongside investment support for firms absorbing dual regulatory costs, before the window to preserve these cross-border production relationships closes.

Written by Jun Du, based on our joint research on UK–EU trade.

Originally published on British Chambers of Commerce, September 14, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Impact of a TB epidemic on worker and firm productivity: the regional perspective from Ukraine
item.description:
Tuberculosis remains a significant regional health burden in Ukraine, with prevalence varying sharply across oblasts. We link regional TB incidence to worker- and firm-level productivity outcomes using administrative records from 2003–2009, finding that higher disease prevalence reduced both worker wages and firm total factor productivity, with substantial spillover effects across neighbouring regions. A 10% reduction in prevalence is estimated to raise GDP by roughly 1.05% — far exceeding the 0.04% of GDP spent on TB control that year, evidence with direct relevance to postwar health and labour policy.

Published in: Journal of Population Economics, 39, article 63 (2026)

Aston Research Explorer | Springer article

item.title: What steel tariffs reveal about the cost of going it alone
item.description:
Using trade data and economic modelling, this piece with Professor Jun Du examines the UK steel tariffs announced in March 2026. It finds the US tariffs already caused steel imports to fall 20% while consumer prices rose around 27%, with 70–80% of the cost passed on to downstream buyers. The UK’s roughly 300,000 downstream steel-using workers carry a heavier burden than its 30,000 primary steelmakers, and the piece argues the UK should coordinate its trade-defence policy with the EU rather than act alone — a joint approach could generate preferential gains worth roughly £482 million a year.

Originally published on UK in a Changing Europe, April 28, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Steel Shield, Budget Blowout
item.description:
The UK government’s plan to double steel tariffs and tighten import quotas is meant to shield domestic steelmakers, but it risks pushing up construction costs sharply. Steel can account for 10–25% of materials costs on large infrastructure projects, and with the UK importing 60–70% of its construction steel, higher tariffs are likely to force expensive redesigns, scope cuts or delays — HS2, already under severe budget strain, is a prime example. The episode illustrates a broader tension in trade policy: protecting an upstream industry (steel) effectively taxes downstream sectors (construction, infrastructure), potentially undercutting the very strategic goals the tariffs are meant to serve.

Originally published on Substack, March 23, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Taiwan’s Tech Triumph: AI Demand Propels Exports to New Heights
item.description:
Taiwan is experiencing explosive export growth — $61.8 billion in October, up 49.7% year-on-year — driven by global demand for AI-related semiconductors and components. The island functions as a critical assembly hub, importing memory chips and integrated circuits from China, South Korea, and the US, then exporting finished products largely to America for data-centre construction. Taiwan’s boom illustrates how technological innovation is reshaping trade patterns, while the EU and UK face a competitive disadvantage from over-regulation, Brexit disruption, high energy costs, and protectionist drift — a reminder that innovation and trade openness go together.

Originally published on Substack, November 10, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Europe’s Rare Earth Quest
item.description:
Europe faces a critical vulnerability in its dependence on Chinese rare-earth elements, which are essential inputs for the automotive industry and renewable energy technologies. China controls around 60% of global production, and a potential export ban could put up to four million German jobs at risk. Europe needs to urgently diversify its supply sources, invest in domestic mining and processing capacity, build strategic reserves, and forge alternative partnerships with producers such as the US, Australia, and Canada.

Originally published on Substack, October 17, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Chips, Curbs & Tariffs
item.description:
China has tightened export controls on rare-earth elements and the technology used to process them, prompting US retaliation through tariffs and software restrictions. The standoff centres on China’s roughly 90% share of rare-earth refining and magnet manufacturing, a chokepoint that leaves semiconductor and defence supply chains dangerously exposed. Companies and governments now face pressure to diversify suppliers, invest in alternative processing capacity, and build strategic reserves. The episode marks a turning point where supply-chain resilience, not just cost, becomes a matter of national and industrial security.

Originally published on Substack, October 13, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: How did the Brexit uncertainty impact services exports of UK firms?
item.description:
Brexit-related uncertainty had a measurable, negative effect on UK firms’ services exports — distinct from, and in some respects larger than, the effect of the tariff and non-tariff barriers that eventually took effect. Using firm-level export data and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we isolate the uncertainty channel from the trade-policy channel by comparing UK firms to a synthetic control built from firms in countries that faced no comparable shock.

Published in: Journal of International Business Policy, 8(1), 80–104

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: Shocked by COVID: Exporting along global value chains
item.description:
COVID-19 hit firms embedded in global value chains differently depending on their position in the chain — upstream suppliers and downstream assemblers absorbed the shock through different channels. Using UK firm-level export data spanning the pandemic, we trace how GVC position shaped the size and persistence of the export shock, and how much of the disruption has since reversed.

Working paper: CEP Discussion Papers dp2105

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: The Future of Electric Vehicles and Technology Leadership
item.description:
The global electric vehicle market has been transformed between 2020 and 2024, with China rising to control around 30% of EV exports on the back of cost advantages and state subsidies, while Germany holds its ground at the high end of the market. That rise has provoked a sharp trade-policy response, with the US and EU imposing substantial tariffs on Chinese EVs in response to the subsidies underpinning their export growth. As the market matures after a period of explosive growth, the piece argues that success will increasingly hinge on how governments balance protectionism against fair competition while still pursuing decarbonisation through coordinated global strategy.

Originally published on Substack, October 8, 2024.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Brexit and the Services Trade—A Longitudinal Analysis
item.description:
Using the OECD-WTO Balanced Trade in Services dataset and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we estimate the impact of Brexit uncertainty on UK services trade from 2016 to 2019. UK services exports fell short of a synthetic no-Brexit counterfactual by an average of US$23.7bn (£18.5bn) a year — a 5.65% reduction — with substantial variation across sectors and destinations. Bilateral exports fell by 8.5% on average; large markets such as Germany and the US were less affected than smaller ones, UK exports to the EU as a whole declined by 6.21%, while, strikingly, exports to Ireland expanded by 21.4%.

Published in: Journal of Service Research, 2024. With Jun Du.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Global value chains in Electric Vehicles
item.description:
With Jun Du, this piece maps the global value chains behind electric vehicle manufacturing and the UK’s position within them, highlighting where the UK carries critical dependencies on other countries for battery and component supply. The underlying working paper, published through Aston University’s Centre for Business Prosperity, frames these dependencies as a resilience and economic-security question as much as a trade one — relevant well beyond the EV sector as governments rethink exposure in strategic supply chains.

Originally published on Substack, September 19, 2024.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Non-tariff measures and productivity of Ukrainian food-processing firms
item.description:
Non-tariff measures imposed by trading partners act as a quality filter on Ukrainian food-processing exporters: firms that clear them see productivity gains, while the compliance costs push less productive firms out of export markets entirely. Using firm-level microdata, we separate this selection effect from the direct within-firm productivity effect of meeting stricter standards — evidence directly relevant to Ukraine’s ongoing agrifood market access negotiations with the EU.

Published in: Journal of Agricultural Economics, 73(1), 234–256

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: Market power, productivity and distribution of wages: theory and evidence with micro data
item.description:
The declining labor share in national income and rising inequality over the last four decades raise questions about their causes. We develop a theoretical model linking the intra-industry distribution of wages to variation in firms’ market power: wages decline with market power if and only if demand elasticity increases with a firm’s output, and trade liberalization expands more productive firms, which raises their bargaining power and lowers labor’s share of revenue. Testing the model on Ukrainian manufacturing firms in 2001–2007, we find that larger firms have more bargaining power relative to workers, that markups rise with output and market size, and that wages rise with productivity but fall with market power — results that hold at both the firm and industry level.

Working paper: IOS Working Paper 387, 2020. With Volodymyr Vakhitov.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Non-tariff measures, quality and exporting: evidence from microdata
item.description:
Non-tariff measures are often treated in policy debate as pure trade friction, but firm-level evidence shows they also act as a quality signal: compliance raises the price premium exporters can command in destination markets, partially offsetting the compliance cost. We quantify this trade-off using product-level export microdata.

Published in: European Review of Agricultural Economics, 47(2), 719–751

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: Political Uncertainty, FDI, and Trade in Intermediate Goods: Evidence From Ukrainian Firms
item.description:
We introduce a text-analysis-based method for measuring policy uncertainty and extend a heterogeneous-firms model with sunk investment costs to derive predictions about how trade policy uncertainty affects firm-specific investment and firms’ decisions to trade intermediate goods. Ukrainian firms faced a stark, mutually exclusive choice of trade regime — an EU free trade agreement or a Russia-led customs union — that we use to measure uncertainty directly. Using firm-product data for Ukrainian manufacturers from 2003 to 2013, we find that reduced uncertainty about the EU FTA sharply increased firm-level FDI inflows and imported intermediate goods from the EU while decreasing FDI from the customs union bloc, with more protected goods responding most strongly.

Working paper: Working paper, 2018. With Jan Stuckatz.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: The evolution of firm-level distributions for Ukrainian manufacturing firms
item.description:
Using unique annual firm-level data for 2001–2009 compiled from Ukraine’s state statistics service, we document rich variation across firms’ characteristics and the macroeconomic volatility — often tied to political turmoil — that accompanies it. Applying functional principal component analysis while accounting for region, industry, trade status, and firm turnover, we show that overall productivity improvements in Ukrainian manufacturing over 2001–2009 varied substantially by industry, trade status, and firm turnover, while regional effects mattered comparatively little.

Published in: Journal of Comparative Economics, 2016. With Kim P. Huynh, David T. Jacho-Chávez, Oleksiy Kryvtsov, and Volodymyr Vakhitov.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Effect of non-tariff measures on extensive and intensive margins of exports in seafood trade
item.description:
Studying global seafood exports from 1996 to 2011, I find that SPS and TBT non-tariff measures affect trade in opposite ways: SPS measures largely increase the extensive margin of exports (more exporters entering) while reducing the intensive margin (less per exporter), whereas TBTs mostly reduce the extensive margin while increasing the intensive margin. Specific trade concerns raised at the WTO have a larger effect on exports than either SPS or TBT notifications alone, both economically and statistically, with substantial heterogeneity across product lines around a consistent central tendency.

Published in: Marine Policy, 2016.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Services liberalization and productivity of manufacturing firms
item.description:
Liberalizing services sectors — telecoms, transport, finance — raises the productivity of the manufacturing firms that use those services as inputs, not just the productivity of the liberalized sector itself. Using Ukrainian firm-level panel data, we trace this indirect productivity channel and show it is large enough to matter for the sequencing of liberalization reforms.

Published in: The Economics of Transition, 23(1), 1–44

Aston Research Explorer
